name: Chloe Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I work underground at the Prairie Hollow potash mine, about a kilometre down. Potash is a salt they turn into fertiliser for farms. I'm the junior on a continuous miner crew, which is a huge machine with a spinning cutting drum on the front that chews the ore off the wall, and I mostly run the conveyor end, watch the cables and learn the controls from my operator, Ray.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real work and that my family's done it. My grandfather was at Prairie Hollow when it opened and my dad's still there on the hoist. What wears me out is the dark and the dust, and that I'm slow on the controls. Ray's patient but I can tell when he wants to take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every few years someone from a city tells us our jobs are finished, and here we are. I'd say it to Dad over Sunday lunch and we'd both have a laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be glad. Daniel and I are getting married in the spring, at St Andrew's, and we want to have kids and stay in this town. Nothing changing is exactly what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep going to work, keep learning the miner from Ray, keep saving. We've got about ten months of our costs saved, plus the little house Daniel's grandparents helped us buy, so we're in a good spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and settled. Like the plan's safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. I don't trust them, and I don't see what I'd need one for. Daniel's sister uses them for everything, even her shopping list, and I think that's a bit sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company already has some automated cutting on the newer panels, where the machine follows the ore on its own and the operator just watches. Ray calls it babysitting. So even if AI is hype, that bit is real.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people from cities keep saying our jobs are finished. I'd laugh about it with my dad over Sunday lunch.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because Daniel and I are marrying in the spring and want kids and to stay in this town. Nothing changing is exactly what I want.
S0.do: Keeps going to work, learning the continuous miner from her operator, and saving. Relies on about ten months of savings and a house bought with family help.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, feeling her plans are safe.
S0.quote: Daniel's sister uses them for everything, even her shopping list, and I think that's a bit sad.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe is a third-generation miner whose life plan is rooted in one town, one church and one mine. She distrusts AI on principle and never uses it. She still notices that automated cutting already exists, separate from AI talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has the right to run its business, but it owes something to the families who built it. At work I'd say we'll manage, like we always have. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried, because the junior jobs go first. Ray's got twenty years and knows every noise the machine makes. I've got two, and the bit I do is the bit a sensor can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work hard so they'd want to keep me. We'd still have the wedding, but I'd tell Daniel to keep saving rather than spending on a big honeymoon. I wouldn't sign up for courses unless the company told me I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit of a cold feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not take a course, if it might keep you on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be bad at it, and then they'd have a reason to let me go. I learn by watching Ray, not from a screen. Grandpa always said you learn a mine with your boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if your job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really the company, they've got to compete. I'd blame the people far away who think everything should be done by machines, the tech companies and the politicians who cheer them on. They've never been down a shaft.

S1.say: I'd say the company has a right to run its business but owes something to the families who built it. At work I'd say we'll manage, like we always have.
S1.think: I'm worried, because junior jobs go first. My operator knows every noise of the machine, and the bit I do is the bit a sensor can do.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and works hard so the company wants to keep her. Goes ahead with the wedding but cuts back the honeymoon, and avoids courses unless required.
S1.quote: I learn by watching Ray, not from a screen. Grandpa always said you learn a mine with your boots.
S1.fieldNote: She sees her own weakness clearly but answers it by working harder in the old way rather than learning new tools. She defends the company's right to compete and blames distant tech firms and politicians instead. Her plans are bent, not broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and that the people pushing it don't care about towns like ours. I'd say it at church, at work, to anyone. I'd want someone to stand up for places like Prairie Hollow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's the end of what my family's done for three generations. Me, my dad, and Ray, all at once. And Daniel's an electrician, so if robots do hands-on work, he's not safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd make the wedding small, just family at St Andrew's and lunch in the hall, and put the rest in savings. We'd put off having kids for a while, which breaks my heart to say. I'd lean on my parents and the church community, and I'd keep working until the last shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake next to Daniel thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save and pray, honestly. I wouldn't know what to learn. I'd hold on to the job, and we'd pay as much off the house as we could, so at least we'd own the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said putting off children breaks your heart. Can you tell me more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum had me at twenty-six and I always thought I'd be the same. We've got names picked, which sounds silly. Waiting because of robots feels like letting someone else run my life.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong and the people pushing it don't care about towns like ours. I'd say it at church and at work, and want someone to stand up for places like Prairie Hollow.
S2.think: It's the end of what my family has done for three generations, for me, my dad and my operator all at once. Daniel's an electrician, so he isn't safe either.
S2.do: Shrinks the wedding to family and a church hall lunch, saves the difference and pays down the house. Delays having children, leans on her parents and church, and works until the last shift.
S2.quote: Waiting because of robots feels like letting someone else run my life.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario threatens not just her job but her family's identity and her plans for children. She has savings and a house, but no idea what to retrain for and no wish to. Her support network is family and church, not government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not enough for a town like ours to adjust. I'd want our local leaders and the church to start talking about it now. People should look after each other, not wait for a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd probably get four years more underground, maybe less. Long enough to get good at the miner just in time for it to stop needing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding as planned, but put off kids by a couple of years. I'd keep working and saving, and pay extra off the house every month. If the company offered an apprenticeship in something solid, maybe I'd go, but not a computer course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the two-year one, but it sits in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for you compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding, mostly. In five years we can still have the day we planned, and maybe one baby before it gets bad. In two, everything gets squeezed. Five gives us time to own the house outright, which matters more to me than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd consider an apprenticeship but not a computer course. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprenticeship is a trade, you learn it from someone who's done it, like I'm doing with Ray. A computer course is sitting in a room being told the machine knows best. I know that sounds stubborn.

S3.say: I'd say five years isn't enough for a town like ours. Local leaders and the church should start talking now, and people should look after each other rather than wait for a cheque.
S3.think: I'd probably get four more years underground at most. That's long enough to get good at the miner just in time for it to stop needing me.
S3.do: Keeps the wedding as planned but delays children by a couple of years. Works, saves and pays extra off the house each month, and might take a company apprenticeship in a trade but not a computer course.
S3.feel: Anxious, a feeling that sits in her stomach.
S3.quote: A computer course is sitting in a room being told the machine knows best.
S3.fieldNote: Five years saves her wedding but not her timeline for children. She is open to learning a trade from a person but not from a screen, and recognises that sounds stubborn. Owning the house outright is her clearest goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time for families and towns to plan, so we'd better not waste it. I'd say people should teach their kids trades and keep the community strong. That's what I'd say at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it feels far away. I'd be thirty-seven, probably with two kids and the house paid off. I'd think about it, but I wouldn't change much yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, nothing really changes. Wedding in the spring, keep working, keep saving, maybe try for a baby in a year or two like we planned. I'd only start looking at other work if the company started cutting crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for my kids than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn something with their hands that people will always want from a person, though I don't know what that is anymore. And to stay close to family, because that's what lasts. I don't have a better answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't change much. Isn't ten years enough time to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I know that. But I like my job and I've only just started. I'd rather have ten good years underground than spend them in a classroom for something that might go too.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time for families and towns to plan, so we shouldn't waste it. People should teach their kids trades and keep the community strong.
S4.think: It feels far away. At thirty-seven I'd probably have two kids and a paid-off house, so I'd think about it but not change much.
S4.do: Goes ahead with the spring wedding, keeps working and saving, and plans to try for a baby in a year or two as before. Would only look at other work if the company started cutting crews.
S4.feel: Uneasy, mostly for her future children.
S4.quote: I'd rather have ten good years underground than spend them in a classroom for something that might go too.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, her plans go ahead almost untouched. She admits she could retrain but chooses not to, valuing the job she loves now. Her worry moves to the children she hasn't had yet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it takes my job, my dad's and Daniel's all at the same time, and we'd have to put off kids. What would help is the company keeping on the families who've been there for generations, maybe as the people who look after the machines, and proper apprenticeships taught by real tradespeople. Not handouts, I want work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the mine means to the town. The mine paid for the hockey rink, the school bus and half the church roof. If it's run by robots from a city office, who's going to fix the church roof?

headlineQuote: If it's run by robots from a city office, who's going to fix the church roof?
portrait: Chloe Zhang is a 27-year-old junior on a continuous miner crew at an underground potash mine, where her grandfather started and her father still works. She is marrying her fiancé Daniel, an electrician, in the spring at their church, and they have about ten months of savings and a house bought with family help. She never uses AI tools and prefers learning from people to learning from screens. She is calm in the quiet picture, uneasy as change grows, and alarmed in the two-year AGI picture, where she'd shrink the wedding and put off having children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take her job, her father's and Daniel's at once and force them to put off having children.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping on long-serving mining families to look after the machines, and real apprenticeships taught by tradespeople rather than handouts.
